title: Buy capacity that fits the traffic
brief: You need model capacity and the invoice must make sense. Traffic may be steady or spiky, users may be waiting or not, and data may or may not be allowed to leave a region. Choose how to buy tokens, then size it.

blocks.text: Five ways to buy tokens on Azure

blocks.title: Capacity and pricing modes
blocks.intro: Dials: traffic predictability and burstiness, p95 latency need, residency boundary, interactive versus asynchronous, cache hit rate and the cost of idle reserved capacity. Prices change often, so use these as structure and plug in your own price sheet.

options.name: Global Standard
options.summary: Pay-as-you-go. Microsoft advises starting here: it launches first when a new model releases, has the lowest price and the broadest region coverage [[r5]].
pros: No commitment and the highest quota
cons: Prompts may be processed in any region, though data at rest stays in the chosen geography
Shared capacity, so latency varies at large steady volume
options.bestWhen: Small or spiky traffic, flexible residency, the newest model.
options.avoidWhen: A strict processing boundary or a tight p95 on large steady volume.

options.name: Priority processing
options.summary: A pay-as-you-go tier with a latency target stated as p50 per 5-minute window, for example 99% above 80 tokens per second for gpt-5.6-sol and gpt-6-sol, 70 for gpt-5.6-terra, 50 for gpt-5.5 and 100 for gpt-5.4-mini. Set on the deployment or per request with `service_tier` (`auto`, `default`, `priority`) [[r10]].
pros: Uses the same quota as standard
cons: A p50 target per window, not a per-request guarantee
Carries a price premium. Check the price sheet
Offered on Global Standard or Data Zone Standard US
options.bestWhen: Bursty or business-hour interactive traffic that needs steadier latency.
options.avoidWhen: Work nobody waits for, or a need for a contractual latency guarantee.

options.name: Provisioned (PTU) with spillover
options.summary: Reserved capacity billed per PTU per hour, or through 1-month or 1-year Azure Reservations. Overflow that returns a non-200 such as 429 can spill to a standard deployment in the same resource [[r6]] [[r7]].
pros: Cached tokens do not consume PTU capacity, so a high cache rate lowers the PTUs you need
cons: Capacity is held and billed whether or not requests arrive
Quota and reservations do not guarantee capacity
PTU-M deployments keep caching but have no cache breakpoints and no `cache_write_tokens`
options.bestWhen: Predictable, high, sustained volume with a latency target.
options.avoidWhen: Small or spiky traffic, where idle capacity costs more than pay-as-you-go.

meta.v: Azure DeepSeek and Meta Llama spillover

options.name: Batch
options.summary: Azure Global Batch and Data Zone Batch cost 50% less than Global Standard, with a 24-hour target, a separate enqueued-token quota and no real-time SLA. OpenAI's Batch API is also 50% off with a `.jsonl` file, one model per file and a 200 MB upload limit [[r5]] [[r12]].
pros: A separate quota keeps it from competing with live traffic
cons: Results arrive within a 24-hour window, so downstream steps must be asynchronous
options.bestWhen: Evaluation, enrichment, embeddings and classification where 24 hours is fine.
options.avoidWhen: Anything a user is waiting for.

options.name: Flex processing
options.summary: Per-request `service_tier: "flex"` on Azure Global Standard at 50% off, with cached-token discounts also applying. It has no latency or service SLA, shares quota with Standard and does not fall back to Standard on its own [[r11]].
pros: Batch-like price with a synchronous API shape
cons: Capacity is preemptible, so 429 can mean no capacity
408 means raise the timeout (the docs use 900 s)
options.bestWhen: Delay-tolerant work that still wants synchronous calls.
options.avoidWhen: You cannot tolerate 429 or 408, or the model lacks Flex support.

blocks.title: PTU sizing
blocks.expr: Normalized TPM = peak RPM x prompt tokens x (1 - cache rate) + output_input_ratio x peak RPM x response tokens;  PTUs = Normalized TPM / input TPM per PTU, rounded up to the model's increment

vars.v: how many input-token equivalents one output token costs, a model constant
model-specific throughput per PTU. Minimum PTUs and ratios vary by model
share of prompt tokens served from cache. Cached tokens do not consume PTU capacity

blocks.example: The documented example (Data Zone Provisioned, 3,400 input TPM per PTU, ratio 8, increment 5): 1,000 RPM with a 200-token prompt and a 20-token response gives 1,000 x 200 + 8 x 1,000 x 20 = 360,000, so 105.88, rounded up to **110 PTUs**. At a 50% cache rate it is 260,000, so 76.47, rounded up to **80 PTUs** [[r7]].

blocks.takeaway: There is no best mode in the abstract. Steady and interactive favors PTU, bursty and interactive favors Priority, delay-tolerant favors Batch, and a boundary favors the zone or regional types.

blocks.title: Capacity mistakes and how you would notice

items.symptom: A 1-year reservation is purchased and the deployment will not create
items.cause: Reservations and quota do not guarantee capacity
items.fix: Create the deployment first, confirm capacity, then buy the reservation

items.symptom: High PTU bill with low utilization
items.cause: Spiky or small traffic leaves held capacity idle
items.fix: Size PTUs for the steady baseline and let spillover or pay-as-you-go absorb peaks. Watch `AzureOpenAIProvisionedManagedUtilizationV2`

items.symptom: 429s on a provisioned deployment at peak
items.cause: Peak exceeds provisioned capacity and no spillover is configured
items.fix: Configure spillover to a standard deployment in the same resource, globally or per request. It does not support Azure DeepSeek or Meta Llama

items.symptom: Flex requests start failing with 400 after a model change
items.cause: From 2026-09-25 unsupported models return 400, and Flex never falls back to Standard on its own
items.fix: Check Flex support per model, handle 400, 408 and 429 explicitly and use a long client timeout

blocks.title: Preview and price notes, checked 2026-10-13
blocks.md: Flex processing is preview on Azure and beta at OpenAI. The Foundry unified model API and AI gateway in Foundry are preview. Price levels are not quoted here because they change. The break-even against pay-as-you-go is PTUs x hourly PTU price x hours versus expected tokens x token price. Reservations only lower the left side and do not guarantee capacity [[r6]] [[r11]].

quiz.q: A workload peaks at 600 requests per minute with 500-token prompts and 50-token responses and no caching. The model's output-to-input ratio is 4, input TPM per PTU is 2,500 and the PTU increment is 5. How many PTUs do you provision?
quiz.hint: Normalized TPM / input TPM per PTU, rounded up to the increment
quiz.explain: Normalized TPM = 600 x 500 + 4 x 600 x 50 = 300,000 + 120,000 = 420,000. Divided by 2,500 gives 168, and rounding up to the next multiple of 5 gives 170. A 40% cache rate would cut the input term to 180,000 and the result to 120 PTUs.

quiz.q: Interactive traffic is steady all day but spikes to 10 times normal for 20 minutes daily. Which capacity plan fits best?
options: Buy PTUs for the full 10x peak so latency stays stable all day, even while capacity sits idle
Move all interactive traffic to Batch, because the daily peak is short and the discount is 50%
Size PTUs for the steady baseline and spill the peak over to a standard deployment
Use Flex for the interactive traffic, because it costs half as much and answers synchronously
quiz.explain: Sizing for the baseline keeps utilization high and spillover handles the short peak at pay-as-you-go prices. A peak-sized PTU purchase leaves most capacity idle. Batch has no real-time SLA. Flex is preemptible with no SLA, so it is wrong for users who are waiting.

quiz.q: Select every true statement about provisioned throughput (PTU).
options: Capacity is held and billed whether or not requests arrive
Cached tokens do not consume PTU capacity
A reservation guarantees capacity in the region
PTU quota is per subscription, region and deployment type
quiz.explain: Held billing, cached tokens and the quota scope are documented. Neither reservations nor quota guarantee capacity. That is why you create the deployment before buying a reservation.

quiz.q: Match each mode to its contract.

pairs.r: Latency target stated as p50 per 5-minute window, billed pay-as-you-go
24-hour target, separate enqueued-token quota and 50% less
Preemptible with no SLA, so 429 can mean no capacity
Capacity held for you and billed hourly or through a reservation

quiz.explain: Each mode sells a different promise. Priority sells steadier latency without commitment, Batch sells a price for delay, Flex sells batch pricing on a synchronous API without guarantees, and PTU sells held capacity.

takeaways: Start from the traffic shape: steady favors PTU, bursty favors Priority, delay-tolerant favors Batch
PTU sizing is a formula. A higher cache rate lowers the PTUs you need
Quota and reservations do not guarantee capacity, so create the deployment first
Spillover turns a provisioned primary plus standard overflow into one plan
Label Flex and the Foundry gateway items as preview, with the date you checked
